lab_title: Vectors and Projectile Motion: From Components to Trajectories
top_level_objectives: Understand that vectors represent quantities with both magnitude and direction, and combine them using tip-to-tail addition
Decompose a vector into perpendicular components and relate magnitude and direction to those components using right-triangle trigonometry
Explain that the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent of one another
Predict how launch angle and initial speed determine a projectile's range, maximum height, and parabolic trajectory

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the concept of a vector as an arrow possessing both length (magnitude) and orientation (direction), distinguishing it from a plain number.
key_visuals: A single bold arrow floating in 3D space with a labeled length and angle
A scalar number (e.g., a temperature readout) shown alongside for contrast
A protractor overlay and a ruler-style scale marking the arrow's magnitude
student_actions: Grab and rotate the arrow to change its direction while watching the angle label update
Stretch the arrow to change its magnitude and observe the length readout
Compare the vector to the adjacent scalar quantity and note what extra information the vector carries

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how two vectors combine into a single resultant using the tip-to-tail method.
key_visuals: Two differently colored vectors placed in the workspace
A dashed guideline snapping the tail of the second vector onto the tip of the first
A third resultant arrow drawn from the start of the first vector to the tip of the second
student_actions: Drag the second vector so its tail meets the tip of the first
Watch the resultant arrow appear and read out its magnitude and direction
Reorder the two vectors and confirm the resultant is unchanged (commutativity)

scenes.brief_purpose: Teach students to break a vector into perpendicular x- and y-components and connect these to right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: A vector overlaid on an x-y coordinate grid
Dropped horizontal and vertical component arrows forming a right triangle with the vector as hypotenuse
Live labels showing magnitude, angle, and the computed components (v·cos and v·sin)
student_actions: Rotate and resize the vector and observe how the component lengths change
Toggle the right-triangle overlay to see the trig relationships between angle, hypotenuse, and legs
Enter a predicted component value and check it against the displayed calculation

scenes.scene_name: The Velocity Vector of a Launch
scenes.brief_purpose: Transition from abstract vectors to physics by treating a projectile's initial velocity as a vector to be decomposed.
key_visuals: A launcher aimed at an adjustable angle with an initial velocity arrow emerging from it
Horizontal and vertical component arrows split from the velocity vector
Sliders for launch speed and launch angle
student_actions: Adjust the launch angle and speed sliders and watch the velocity components update
Identify which component is horizontal and which is vertical for a given launch
Predict the horizontal and vertical components before revealing the computed values

scenes.scene_name: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the central insight that horizontal and vertical motions evolve independently.
key_visuals: A launched projectile with a persistent horizontal velocity arrow (constant length) and a changing vertical velocity arrow
A ghost object moving in pure horizontal motion and another in pure vertical (dropped) motion, side by side with the projectile
A gravity indicator acting only on the vertical component
student_actions: Launch the projectile and watch the horizontal arrow stay constant while the vertical arrow shrinks, reverses, and grows
Compare the projectile's fall timing to the separately dropped ghost object
Note when the vertical component reaches zero at maximum height

scenes.brief_purpose: Show that the parabola emerges from combining constant horizontal velocity with uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
key_visuals: The full parabolic path traced as a glowing curve
Motion-diagram dots spaced evenly in x but with changing vertical spacing
Component arrows attached to the projectile at several points along the arc
student_actions: Step through the flight frame-by-frame and observe equal horizontal spacing versus uneven vertical spacing
Watch how the two independent motions sum to form the curved path
Identify the apex where vertical velocity is zero

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students experiment with launch parameters to discover how angle and speed control range and maximum height.
key_visuals: A target field with markers for range and a height gauge
Multiple overlaid trajectories from different launch angles at the same speed
A readout panel showing range, maximum height, and flight time
student_actions: Vary the launch angle to find the angle that maximizes range
Increase launch speed and observe the proportional effect on range and height
Compare complementary angles (e.g., 30 and 60 degrees) and note they produce the same range
